strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 30 attacks reproduced with high fidelity (+0.26 pp mean ASR deviation) across 10 victim models, with thorough ablations on with-repo vs. no-repo (+19.8% improvement)
Well-designed three-layer architecture (JBF-LIB, JBF-FORGE, JBF-EVAL) with clear separation of concerns and explicit framework contracts enabling modularity and reuse (82.5% code reuse)
Addresses a genuine, practical problem: benchmarks rapidly become stale as jailbreak attacks evolve, and JBF offers a scalable solution for maintaining living benchmarks

Valuable attack-model interaction insights (Section 5): reveals mechanism-specific bypasses, non-transferability of many attacks, and model-specific format sensitivity that wouldn't be visible with smaller attack suites
Sound technical execution with reasonable design choices: bounded loop approach with deterministic execution, detailed framework contracts, comprehensive documentation enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is applying mature paper-to-code generation techniques to a new domain; the multi-agent planner-coder-auditor workflow is creative but not theoretically novel

Robustness concerns inadequately addressed: two large outliers (SCP -11.8%, ISA -16.0%) lack deep explanation; enhanced refinement pass appears as post-hoc patch when ASR gaps occur; system heavily depends on specific LLM agents whose future availability is uncertain

Incomplete analysis of core design decisions: Figure 5 shows weak correlation (r=0.186, p=0.325) between iteration count and attack performance, yet bounded loop with T=5 iterations is retained without justification; no computational cost analysis provided

Domain specificity limits impact: system narrowly tailored to jailbreak attacks on LLMs with AdvBench/JailbreakBench results; reproducibility requires papers in these specific formats; contributions are valuable but specialized for ICML's broad audience

Methodological limitations: standardized evaluation uses only GPT-4o judge without robustness testing; with-repo results show strong dependence on reference code availability (limiting generalizability); test gate runs only one sample (may miss subtle bugs); no statistical significance testing

Presentation and clarity issues: paper is dense across multiple subsystems; critical with-repo ablation appears relatively late; very long agent instruction prompts in appendices; some technical details underexplained (victim-as-target special case, auditor fidelity criteria, why enhanced refinement uses different agent)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap between rapidly evolving jailbreak attacks and static benchmarks
Thoughtful multi-agent architecture (planner-coder-auditor) with iterative refinement and clear separation of concerns between attack generation and evaluation
Comprehensive evaluation at scale: 30 attacks × 10 models with multiple fidelity verification methods (ASR, traces, semantic audit, mechanism-level checks)
Impressive high-fidelity reproduction: mean ASR deviation +0.26pp with only 2/30 attacks showing >10% negative gaps
Significant practical impact: 28 min synthesis vs. weeks/months manual work, 58% LOC reduction, 82.5% code reuse
Novel empirical insights on attack-model interactions revealing mechanism-specific vulnerabilities and model-dependent attack effectiveness patterns
Honest treatment of limitations, clear scope boundaries, and thoughtful future work directions
Strong reproducibility support: detailed algorithms, complete agent prompts in appendices, token usage statistics, and code release commitment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques without fundamental algorithmic innovation
Heavy dependence on proprietary expensive LLMs (Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex) with demonstrated sensitivity (-54% with weaker planner), raising sustainability concerns
Incomplete analysis of failure cases: large negative gaps (SCP -11.8%, ISA -16.0%) remain inadequately explained; enhanced refinement only partially resolves ISA
Narrow scope limited to jailbreak attacks only; generalizability to other adversarial benchmarking domains unclear
Experimental design issues: with-repo ablation on only 5 attacks, compression ratio metric potentially misleading, multi-model evaluation uses single default parameters
Insufficient cost analysis: token usage reported but practical dollar costs and comparison to manual integration omitted
Inadequate dual-use risk mitigation: acknowledges barrier-lowering but proposes only vague responsible deployment without concrete safeguards
Reproducibility concerns: API brittleness, non-determinism inadequately characterized, evaluation limited to single judge (GPT-4o) without testing alternatives
No empirical comparison to existing benchmarking frameworks (JailbreakBench, EasyJailbreak, OpenRT); unclear how JBF practically improves upon these
